days.title: How 4 YOE interviews work + roadmap
days.exp: Interviewers at ~4 years expect ownership of a vertical slice, production debugging, and clear trade-offs — not Staff-level CLR trivia. Typical loop: screen → technical (C#/ASP.NET/SQL) → small system design → behavioral/resume.
pts: **Junior vs 4 YOE vs Staff:** juniors show syntax; mid shows patterns + edge cases + tests; staff shapes org-wide architecture.
Product companies push design + debugging; consultancies push broad SOLID/SQL/Azure coverage.
Prepare **5 STAR stories**: incident, performance win, disagreement, mentoring, deadline trade-off.
Every resume bullet needs: your role, architecture sketch, hardest bug, metric, what you'd redo.
Prep cadence: 2–3 weeks focused on Parts in this path, then mock interviews.

qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Week 1: async, DI, ASP.NET pipeline, EF/SQL (N+1, indexes, isolation). Week 2: security, messaging, caching, observability, three system designs, and STAR/resume drills. Daily: 30–45 min flashcards + one design sketch.

days.title: C# essentials — IEnumerable, boxing, Span, records
days.exp: Language questions at 4 YOE test whether you know where work runs (memory vs SQL) and allocation cost — not trivia for its own sake.
pts: **IEnumerable** = in-memory; **IQueryable** = expression tree for providers (EF→SQL); **IAsyncEnumerable** = async streams (`await foreach`).
**Boxing** copies a value type to the heap (`object`/interface) — prefer generics (`List<int>`).
`Span<T>` is a stack-only view (no alloc for slices); cannot be a class field or cross `await` — use `Memory<T>` then.
`readonly struct` for small immutable values; `record` for value-equality DTOs/events.
Mention modern C#: pattern matching, `required`, NRTs, `await using`.
days.code:
int x = 42;
object boxed = x;           // BOX — heap alloc
int y = (int)boxed;         // UNBOX_ANY

Span<byte> slice = buffer.AsSpan(0, 16); // no new array
IQueryable<Order> q = db.Orders.Where(o => o.Total > 100); // SQL later

qa.q: IEnumerable vs IQueryable — when does each execute?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** IEnumerable operators run in-process when enumerated. IQueryable builds an expression tree; the provider (EF) translates to SQL when enumerated/materialized (ToList, First, etc.). Mixing them poorly can pull too much data into memory.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Boxing allocates a System.Object header (16 bytes on x64) on the managed heap and copies the value type bytes into it. Span<T> is a ref struct allocated strictly on the execution stack, providing contiguous memory access without heap allocation or array copying.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Boxing inside a high-throughput loop generates thousands of ephemeral Gen 0 objects, triggering frequent GC pauses and thread pool delays. Fix: use generic collection interfaces (IList<T>) and Span<T>/Memory<T> for byte slicing.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Span<T> provides zero-allocation performance, but ref struct rules forbid storing it on the heap, as class fields, or across async await points (where Memory<T> must be used).

qa.q: When would you use Span<T> and what are its limits?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Use Span for slicing/parsing contiguous memory without allocations. Limits: ref struct — can't be stored on the heap, can't be class fields, can't be used across await. Use Memory<T> when you need to hold the view longer.

days.title: Async — state machine, ValueTask, deadlocks, starvation
days.exp: `async` builds a state machine; it does not spawn a thread. At 4 YOE you must diagnose deadlocks and thread-pool starvation in production language.
pts: Await I/O; don't block with `.Result` / `.Wait()` on ASP.NET request threads.
**ValueTask<T>** for hot paths that often complete synchronously — await once; don't spray everywhere.
ASP.NET Core has no sync context by default; `ConfigureAwait(false)` still matters in libraries.
**Thread-pool starvation:** sync-over-async or long CPU on pool threads → request queueing.
Propagate **CancellationToken** from controller → service → EF/HttpClient.

qa.q: Why can .Result deadlock, and how do you fix it?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** If a SynchronizationContext must resume the continuation but the thread is blocked waiting for the task, you deadlock. Fix: async all the way with await; never block in UI/legacy sync contexts. In ASP.NET Core prefer await over Result always.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Async methods compile into an IAsyncStateMachine struct managed by the AsyncMethodBuilder. Awaiting an uncompleted task yields execution back to the caller. Blocking with .Result on a thread bound to a SynchronizationContext causes deadlocks when the continuation waits for the blocked thread.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Sync-over-async (.Result or .Wait()) on ASP.NET request threads rapidly exhausts thread pool threads, leading to HTTP 503 gateway timeouts and request queuing under load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Async all the way preserves thread pool scalability, but requires passing CancellationToken through all layers and avoiding sync blocking methods everywhere.

qa.a:

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Async methods compile into an IAsyncStateMachine struct managed by the AsyncMethodBuilder. Awaiting an uncompleted task yields execution back to the caller. Blocking with .Result on a thread bound to a SynchronizationContext causes deadlocks when the continuation waits for the blocked thread.

days.title: DI lifetimes, HttpClient, Options pattern
days.exp: Captive dependencies and socket exhaustion are classic 4 YOE gotchas. Know Transient/Scoped/Singleton cold.
pts: **Transient** every resolve; **Scoped** per request; **Singleton** app lifetime.
Never inject Scoped (DbContext) into Singleton — captive dependency.
In `BackgroundService`, use `IServiceScopeFactory.CreateScope()`.
Never `new HttpClient()` per call — use `IHttpClientFactory` + Polly (retry/circuit/timeout).
`IOptions` / `IOptionsSnapshot` / `IOptionsMonitor` — don't inject raw `IConfiguration` everywhere.

qa.q: Why can't you inject DbContext into a Singleton?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** DbContext is scoped. Captured by a singleton it lives for the app lifetime, becoming shared/unsafe across requests (threading + disposed state). Create a scope per unit of work via IServiceScopeFactory.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Transient creates a new instance on every request; Scoped creates one instance per HTTP request container; Singleton lives for the app domain lifespan. Capturing a Scoped service inside a Singleton captures the DbContext across requests, causing concurrency bugs.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Instantiating new HttpClient() instances manually causes socket exhaustion in OS TIME_WAIT state under high concurrency. Fix: register typed clients with IHttpClientFactory to manage handler lifetimes and DNS refresh.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** IHttpClientFactory prevents socket leaks and manages DNS rotation, but requires explicit Polly retry and circuit breaker policies to prevent cascade failures during downstream outages.

qa.q: Why is IHttpClientFactory preferred?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** It manages handler lifetimes and DNS refresh, avoiding socket exhaustion from disposing HttpClient too often or holding one forever. Enables named/typed clients and resilience policies.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Transient creates a new instance on every request; Scoped creates one instance per HTTP request container; Singleton lives for the app domain lifespan. Capturing a Scoped service inside a Singleton captures the DbContext across requests, causing concurrency bugs.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Instantiating new HttpClient() instances manually causes socket exhaustion in OS TIME_WAIT state under high concurrency. Fix: register typed clients with IHttpClientFactory to manage handler lifetimes and DNS refresh.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** IHttpClientFactory prevents socket leaks and manages DNS rotation, but requires explicit Polly retry and circuit breaker policies to prevent cascade failures during downstream outages.

days.exp: Design questions at 4 YOE are about practical APIs: versioning, pagination, idempotency keys, and status codes — not HATEOAS purity contests.
pts: Resources + verbs: `POST/GET/PATCH /orders`; filter via query.

REST vs gRPC vs GraphQL: public HTTP vs internal contracts vs flexible queries (with N+1 risk).

days.title: EF Core & SQL — N+1, indexes, AsNoTracking
days.exp: Data access is where mid-senior candidates separate themselves: N+1, plans, and read vs write patterns.
pts: N+1: fix with `Include`, projections, split queries, or Dapper joins.
Indexes: clustered vs nonclustered; seek vs scan; covering `INCLUDE`.

qa.q: What is the N+1 problem and how do you fix it in EF?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Loading a collection then lazy-loading a navigation per row causes 1+N queries. Fix with Include/ThenInclude, Select projections, AsSplitQuery for big graphs, or explicit SQL joins. Verify with logging or a profiler.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Transient creates a new instance on every request; Scoped creates one instance per HTTP request container; Singleton lives for the app domain lifespan. Capturing a Scoped service inside a Singleton captures the DbContext across requests, causing concurrency bugs.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Instantiating new HttpClient() instances manually causes socket exhaustion in OS TIME_WAIT state under high concurrency. Fix: register typed clients with IHttpClientFactory to manage handler lifetimes and DNS refresh.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** IHttpClientFactory prevents socket leaks and manages DNS rotation, but requires explicit Polly retry and circuit breaker policies to prevent cascade failures during downstream outages.

qa.q: When do you use AsNoTracking?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Read-only queries where you won't Update/SaveChanges. Skipping tracking reduces memory and CPU. Don't use it if you need to mutate and persist the same instances.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Boxing allocates a System.Object header (16 bytes on x64) on the managed heap and copies the value type bytes into it. Span<T> is a ref struct allocated strictly on the execution stack, providing contiguous memory access without heap allocation or array copying.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Span<T> provides zero-allocation performance, but ref struct rules forbid storing it on the heap, as class fields, or across async await points (where Memory<T> must be used).

days.title: Transactions, isolation, concurrency, soft delete
days.exp: Isolation levels and optimistic concurrency are favorite 4 YOE topics — especially RCSI vs locking.
pts: Read Committed default; Snapshot/RCSI lets readers avoid blocking writers (version store).
Serializable prevents phantoms but costs blocking — use sparingly.
EF: `BeginTransactionAsync` + execution strategy for transient retries.
**RowVersion** / concurrency token → `DbUpdateConcurrencyException` → reload/merge.
Soft delete via global filters; watch unique indexes on 'deleted' rows.

qa.q: What does READ COMMITTED SNAPSHOT buy you?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Row versioning so readers don't take shared locks that block writers (and vice versa) for typical read committed scenarios. Trade-off: tempdb version store cost and different anomaly profile — know it isn't full serializability.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Transient creates a new instance on every request; Scoped creates one instance per HTTP request container; Singleton lives for the app domain lifespan. Capturing a Scoped service inside a Singleton captures the DbContext across requests, causing concurrency bugs.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Instantiating new HttpClient() instances manually causes socket exhaustion in OS TIME_WAIT state under high concurrency. Fix: register typed clients with IHttpClientFactory to manage handler lifetimes and DNS refresh.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** IHttpClientFactory prevents socket leaks and manages DNS rotation, but requires explicit Polly retry and circuit breaker policies to prevent cascade failures during downstream outages.

qa.q: How do you handle optimistic concurrency in EF Core?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Add a RowVersion/timestamp (or token) configured as concurrency token. On SaveChanges conflict, catch DbUpdateConcurrencyException, reload database values, merge or ask the user, retry.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** EF Core builds an Expression Tree, translates it via the relational SQL provider into a parameterized T-SQL query, and materializes entities into the DbContext Change Tracker. N+1 queries occur when navigating un-included navigation properties in a loop.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Executing queries without AsNoTracking() in read-only APIs forces EF Core to keep snapshot copies of all returned entities in memory, causing high RAM usage and CPU tracking overhead.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** AsNoTracking() speeds up read queries by 20-30% and reduces memory footprint, but disables identity resolution and automatic change tracking for updates.

days.title: Messaging — RabbitMQ vs Kafka, outbox, saga
days.exp: Know when to pick a broker, what partitions mean, and how to avoid dual-write bugs.
pts: RabbitMQ: routing, work queues, push consumers.
Kafka: log, partitions = parallelism/ordering, consumer groups, replay.
**Outbox:** DB + outbox row same transaction; publisher drains — at-least-once without lost events.
**Saga:** multi-step business flow with compensations (choreography vs orchestration).
SignalR: WebSockets + fallback; scale-out via Redis/Azure SignalR.

qa.q: When do you choose Kafka over RabbitMQ?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** High-throughput event streams, replay/retention, partition-scaled consumers, and log-oriented processing. Choose RabbitMQ for complex routing, classic work queues, and lower operational complexity at moderate volume.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Kafka uses an append-only commit log partitioned across brokers where consumer offsets track read positions. Outbox pattern solves dual-write by storing domain changes and event messages in the same relational DB transaction, guaranteeing at-least-once delivery.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Publishing directly to a message broker during an HTTP request without Outbox pattern risks losing events if the broker call fails after DB commit (or vice-versa).

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Outbox guarantees reliable message delivery without distributed 2PC transactions, but requires idempotent consumer processing and an asynchronous background publisher worker.

qa.q: What problem does the outbox pattern solve?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Dual-write: updating DB and publishing a message separately can lose one side on failure. Outbox writes the event in the same DB transaction; a process publishes later, yielding reliable at-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Transient creates a new instance on every request; Scoped creates one instance per HTTP request container; Singleton lives for the app domain lifespan. Capturing a Scoped service inside a Singleton captures the DbContext across requests, causing concurrency bugs.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Instantiating new HttpClient() instances manually causes socket exhaustion in OS TIME_WAIT state under high concurrency. Fix: register typed clients with IHttpClientFactory to manage handler lifetimes and DNS refresh.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** IHttpClientFactory prevents socket leaks and manages DNS rotation, but requires explicit Polly retry and circuit breaker policies to prevent cascade failures during downstream outages.

days.title: Observability & resilience — OTel, latency, Polly
days.exp: Logs + metrics + traces, correlated by trace id. Plus timeouts, retries, and circuit breakers used correctly.
pts: OpenTelemetry hooks .NET `Activity`, `Meter`, `ILogger`.
Latency checklist: P95/P99, traces, ThreadPool/GC counters, N+1, sync-over-async.
Polly: timeout, retry (transient only), circuit breaker, bulkhead — retries must be idempotent.
Health: live vs ready (DB/Redis/bus).
Don't log secrets; prefer structured Serilog properties.

qa.q: How do you debug increasing API latency over days?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Check metrics (P95, errors, dependency times), distributed traces for slow spans, runtime counters (thread pool queue, GC), recent deploys/config, and classics: N+1, missing index, sync-over-async, cache stampede, chatty logging.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Boxing allocates a System.Object header (16 bytes on x64) on the managed heap and copies the value type bytes into it. Span<T> is a ref struct allocated strictly on the execution stack, providing contiguous memory access without heap allocation or array copying.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Boxing inside a high-throughput loop generates thousands of ephemeral Gen 0 objects, triggering frequent GC pauses and thread pool delays. Fix: use generic collection interfaces (IList<T>) and Span<T>/Memory<T> for byte slicing.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Span<T> provides zero-allocation performance, but ref struct rules forbid storing it on the heap, as class fields, or across async await points (where Memory<T> must be used).

qa.q: When should a retry policy NOT retry?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** On non-transient errors (400 validation, 401/403), non-idempotent POSTs without idempotency keys, and after a circuit is open. Retry timeouts/5xx/connection resets with jittered backoff.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Operating When should a retry policy NOT retry? at scale requires understanding the runtime lifecycle, memory allocations, and underlying execution constraints. The underlying framework or storage engine optimizes execution when contracts are explicitly preserved.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Un-handled edge cases in When should a retry policy NOT retry? under high concurrent traffic can lead to performance degradation, unhandled exceptions, or unexpected memory growth. Always enforce defensive validation and error handling.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Choosing this implementation approach balances developer velocity and system performance. Senior engineers evaluate latency, operational overhead, and maintenance costs before committing.

days.exp: At 4 YOE, compare hosting options and describe a safe deploy/rollback path.
pts: App Service: faster PaaS path, less ops.

qa.q: App Service vs AKS for a single .NET API?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Default to App Service for one API needing speed-to-prod and managed scaling. Choose AKS when you run many services, need custom networking/sidecars, or already operate Kubernetes. Don't adopt K8s for resume points alone.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Transient creates a new instance on every request; Scoped creates one instance per HTTP request container; Singleton lives for the app domain lifespan. Capturing a Scoped service inside a Singleton captures the DbContext across requests, causing concurrency bugs.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Instantiating new HttpClient() instances manually causes socket exhaustion in OS TIME_WAIT state under high concurrency. Fix: register typed clients with IHttpClientFactory to manage handler lifetimes and DNS refresh.

days.title: System design drills + behavioral finals
days.exp: Practice mid-senior designs (~35 min): URL shortener, notifications, rate limiter, checkout. Close with STAR stories.
pts: **URL shortener:** hash/counter IDs, Redis cache, store, rate limit, async analytics.
**Notifications:** channels, templates, outbox, retries, preferences, idempotency.
**Rate limiter:** token bucket/sliding window in Redis; 429 semantics.
**Checkout:** reserve inventory → pay → order; saga/compensations; payment idempotency.
Behavioral: Situation → Task → Action (technical) → Result (numbers).

viz.note: Whiteboard drill: pick one design daily. State requirements, API, data model, bottlenecks, and what you'd monitor in prod.

qa.q: Outline a notification service for email/SMS/push.
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** API accepts notify requests with idempotency keys; persist outbox; workers per channel with retries/DLQ; template service; user preferences; provider adapters; metrics on send success/latency; never block the upstream order flow on provider latency.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** EF Core builds an Expression Tree, translates it via the relational SQL provider into a parameterized T-SQL query, and materializes entities into the DbContext Change Tracker. N+1 queries occur when navigating un-included navigation properties in a loop.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Executing queries without AsNoTracking() in read-only APIs forces EF Core to keep snapshot copies of all returned entities in memory, causing high RAM usage and CPU tracking overhead.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** AsNoTracking() speeds up read queries by 20-30% and reduces memory footprint, but disables identity resolution and automatic change tracking for updates.

qa.q: Give a STAR story structure for a production incident.
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Situation: symptom + blast radius. Task: your ownership. Action: how you diagnosed (metrics/traces), mitigated, fixed root cause. Result: MTTR, error rate drop, follow-up (test, alert, postmortem).

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Async methods compile into an IAsyncStateMachine struct managed by the AsyncMethodBuilder. Awaiting an uncompleted task yields execution back to the caller. Blocking with .Result on a thread bound to a SynchronizationContext causes deadlocks when the continuation waits for the blocked thread.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Sync-over-async (.Result or .Wait()) on ASP.NET request threads rapidly exhausts thread pool threads, leading to HTTP 503 gateway timeouts and request queuing under load.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Async all the way preserves thread pool scalability, but requires passing CancellationToken through all layers and avoiding sync blocking methods everywhere.

days.title: Advanced Memory Diagnostics, GC Internals & Profiling
days.exp: Production debugging at 4 YOE requires explaining Server vs Workstation GC, Gen 0/1/2, LOH/POH, memory leak diagnosis using dotnet-dump, dotnet-gcdump, and memory profilers.
pts: **Server GC** (high throughput, multi-heap per core) vs **Workstation GC** (low footprint, responsive UI).
**Gen 0/1** (ephemeral), **Gen 2** (long-lived), **LOH** (>85,000 bytes or double arrays), **POH** (pinned objects for native I/O).
Common memory leaks: static event handler subscriptions, unmanaged resources not disposed, captive scoped dependencies, `Timer` callbacks.
CLI tools: `dotnet-counters` for real-time monitoring, `dotnet-gcdump` for quick object counts, `dotnet-dump` for full heap dumps & `sos` inspection.
GC tuning: `GCLargeObjectHeapCompensate`, `GCHeapHardLimit`, background vs non-concurrent GC.

qa.q: How do you diagnose a memory leak in a production ASP.NET Core Linux container?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** 1. Monitor GC heap size and Gen 2 collection rate via dotnet-counters. 2. Capture a dump using dotnet-gcdump or dotnet-dump collect. 3. Analyze dump using dotnet-dump analyze with dumpheap -stat to find top types by count/size. 4. Trace gcroot (gcroot <address>) to find what static or long-lived object holds the references.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Boxing allocates a System.Object header (16 bytes on x64) on the managed heap and copies the value type bytes into it. Span<T> is a ref struct allocated strictly on the execution stack, providing contiguous memory access without heap allocation or array copying.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Boxing inside a high-throughput loop generates thousands of ephemeral Gen 0 objects, triggering frequent GC pauses and thread pool delays. Fix: use generic collection interfaces (IList<T>) and Span<T>/Memory<T> for byte slicing.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Span<T> provides zero-allocation performance, but ref struct rules forbid storing it on the heap, as class fields, or across async await points (where Memory<T> must be used).

qa.q: What is the difference between Large Object Heap (LOH) and Pinned Object Heap (POH)?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** LOH holds objects >85,000 bytes (and large double arrays). It is not compacted by default during Gen 2 collections to avoid high copy cost, leading to fragmentation. POH (introduced in .NET 5) holds objects explicitly pinned for native/interop I/O, preventing GC compaction from having to update native pointers.

days.title: CQRS, MediatR & Integration Event Patterns
days.exp: Mid-senior roles test your understanding of separating reads from writes, pipeline behaviors, and reliable inter-service event communication.
pts: **CQRS** (Command Query Responsibility Segregation): separate mutating commands from read-optimized queries.
**MediatR**: in-process mediator pattern for decoupling controllers from business logic & cross-cutting concerns (validation, logging, transactions).
**MediatR Pipeline Behaviors**: intercept requests for logging, fluent validation (`IPipelineBehavior<TRequest, TResponse>`), and performance timing.
**Domain Events** (in-transaction synchronous/async handlers within domain boundary) vs **Integration Events** (asynchronous messages published across microservice boundaries via broker).
Outbox pattern + Change Data Capture (CDC/Debezium) or outbox processor to guarantee zero lost events.

qa.q: When is full CQRS (with separate read/write databases) worth the complexity?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** When read and write workloads have radically different scale requirements (e.g., 100:1 read-to-write ratio), or when read models require complex aggregated denormalization (Elasticsearch/Redis) while write models require strict transactional integrity (ACID RDBMS). For simple CRUD, full CQRS adds unnecessary operational overhead.

days.title: Enterprise Auth — OAuth2, SCIM 2.0, Rate Limiting & Token Security
days.exp: Senior interviews for enterprise SaaS expect deep knowledge of identity provisioning (SCIM), OAuth2/OIDC token security, and API rate limiting.
pts: **SCIM 2.0** (System for Cross-domain Identity Management): standardized REST API (`/Users`, `/Groups`) for automated user provisioning/deprovisioning from Okta/Entra ID.
**Token Security**: JWT verification (issuer, audience, signature key rollover, expiry, `nbf`), token revocation strategies (Redis blacklist / token version counter in DB).
**ASP.NET Core Rate Limiting** (built-in in .NET 7/8/9+): Fixed Window, Sliding Window, Token Bucket, Concurrency Limiter.
**Security Headers & API Defense**: CORS origin policies, CSP, HSTS, rate-limiting HTTP headers (`X-RateLimit-Limit`, `Retry-After`).
**SCIM Security**: Bearer tokens, tenant isolation, handling patch updates (`PATCH /Users/{id}`).

qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Instead of custom sync scripts, SCIM 2.0 provides standard JSON REST schemas for IdPs (Azure AD/Entra ID, Okta) to automatically push user creations, attribute updates, and soft/hard deprovisioning directly into the SaaS platform.
